claim: CNNMs are an evolutionarily conserved family of magnesium transporters.
source: Cystathionine-β-synthase (CBS)-pair domain divalent metal cation transport mediators (CNNMs) are an evolutionarily conserved family of magnesium transporters.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of CNNMs.

claim: CNNMs promote efflux of Mg2+ ions on their own.
source: They promote efflux of Mg2+ ions on their own and influx of divalent cations when expressed with the transient receptor potential ion channel subfamily M member 7 (TRPM7).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: CNNMs promote influx of divalent cations when expressed with TRPM7.
source: They promote efflux of Mg2+ ions on their own and influx of divalent cations when expressed with the transient receptor potential ion channel subfamily M member 7 (TRPM7).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: ARL15 has been identified as a CNNM-binding partner.
source: Recently, ADP-ribosylation factor-like GTPase 15 (ARL15) has been identified as CNNM-binding partner and an inhibitor of divalent cation influx by TRPM7.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by binding experiments shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: ARL15 is an inhibitor of divalent cation influx by TRPM7.
source: Recently, ADP-ribosylation factor-like GTPase 15 (ARL15) has been identified as CNNM-binding partner and an inhibitor of divalent cation influx by TRPM7.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 7B-E.

claim: ARL15 binds GTP.
source: Here, we characterize ARL15 as a GTP and CNNM-binding protein and demonstrate that ARL15 also inhibits CNNM2 Mg2+ efflux.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by NMR and ITC experiments in Figure 1.

claim: ARL15 inhibits CNNM2 Mg2+ efflux.
source: Here, we characterize ARL15 as a GTP and CNNM-binding protein and demonstrate that ARL15 also inhibits CNNM2 Mg2+ efflux.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the Mg2+ efflux assay in Figure 7A.

claim: The crystal structure of a complex between ARL15 and CNNM2 CBS-pair domain was determined.
source: The crystal structure of a complex between ARL15 and CNNM2 CBS-pair domain reveals the molecular basis for binding and allowed the identification of mutations that specifically block binding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and the structure is shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ARL15 R95A mutant failed to inhibit CNNM and TRPM7 transport of Mg2+ and Zn2+ ions.
source: A binding deficient ARL15 mutant, R95A, failed to inhibit CNNM and TRPM7 transport of Mg2+ and Zn2+ ions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by experiments in Figure 7.

claim: ARL15 and PRLs compete for binding CNNM.
source: Structural analysis and binding experiments with phosphatase of regenerating liver 2 (PRL2 or PTP4A2) showed that ARL15 and PRLs compete for binding CNNM to coordinate regulation of ion transport by CNNM and TRPM7.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by ITC and NMR experiments in Figure 6.

claim: Mg2+ is the most abundant intracellular divalent cation.
source: Magnesium (Mg2+) is the most abundant intracellular divalent cation and essential for key cellular processes such as energy production and protein synthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Mg2+ is essential for key cellular processes such as energy production and protein synthesis.
source: Magnesium (Mg2+) is the most abundant intracellular divalent cation and essential for key cellular processes such as energy production and protein synthesis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: TRPM7 is a ubiquitously expressed ion channel with a C-terminal kinase domain.
source: TRPM7 is a ubiquitously expressed ion channel with a C-terminal kinase domain also involved in Ca2+ homeostasis and Zn2+ transport (Monteilh-Zoller et al., 2003; Clark et al., 2006; Wei et al., 2009; Visser et al., 2013; Krapivinsky et al., 2014; Mittermeier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: TRPM7 is involved in Ca2+ homeostasis and Zn2+ transport.
source: TRPM7 is a ubiquitously expressed ion channel with a C-terminal kinase domain also involved in Ca2+ homeostasis and Zn2+ transport (Monteilh-Zoller et al., 2003; Clark et al., 2006; Wei et al., 2009; Visser et al., 2013; Krapivinsky et al., 2014; Mittermeier et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: CNNMs are mutated in genetic diseases linked to Mg2+ uptake or transport.
source: CNNMs are a widely conserved family of integral membrane proteins and mutated in genetic diseases linked to Mg2+ uptake or transport (Wang et al., 2003; Funato and Miki, 2019; Giménez-Mascarell et al., 2019; Chen and Gehring, 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: TRPM7 and CNNMs function together to mediate divalent cation influx as a trimeric complex with ARL15.
source: Recently, TRPM7 and CNNMs were found to function together to mediate divalent cation influx as a trimeric complex with ADP-ribosylation factor-like GTPase 15 (ARL15) (Zolotarov et al., 2021; Kollewe et al., 2021; Bai et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: CNNMs employ the TRPM7 channel for Mg2+ uptake.
source: Mg2+ uptake experiments demonstrated that CNNMs employ the TRPM7 channel and that, in the absence of the channel, CNNM2 and CNNM4 can lower intracellular Mg2+ levels (Bai et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: In the absence of TRPM7, CNNM2 and CNNM4 can lower intracellular Mg2+ levels.
source: Mg2+ uptake experiments demonstrated that CNNMs employ the TRPM7 channel and that, in the absence of the channel, CNNM2 and CNNM4 can lower intracellular Mg2+ levels (Bai et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: ARL15 binds the C-terminal portion of CNNM2.
source: Experiments showed that ARL15 binds the C-terminal portion of CNNM2 and increases CNNM3/TRPM7 protein complex formation to reduce TRPM7 activity (Hardy et al., 2023; Zolotarov et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ARL15 increases CNNM3/TRPM7 protein complex formation to reduce TRPM7 activity.
source: Experiments showed that ARL15 binds the C-terminal portion of CNNM2 and increases CNNM3/TRPM7 protein complex formation to reduce TRPM7 activity (Hardy et al., 2023; Zolotarov et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ARL15 is associated with several metabolic traits including disorders of lipid metabolism.
source: ARL15 is a member of the RAS superfamily of small GTPases and associated with several metabolic traits including disorders of lipid metabolism (Richards et al., 2009; Rocha et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Genome-wide association studies have found associations between ARL15 and coronary heart disease, kidney disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and diabetes.
source: Genome-wide association studies have found associations with coronary heart disease, kidney disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and diabetes (Gorski et al., 2017; Negi et al., 2013; DIAbetes Genetics Replication And Meta-analysis (DIAGRAM) Consortium et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ARL15 is most closely related to ARF and ARL GTPases within the GTPase superfamily.
source: Within the GTPase superfamily, ARL15 is most closely related to ADP-ribosylation factor (ARF) and ARF-like (ARL) GTPases.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a classification of ARL15.

claim: ARF GTPases are often involved in membrane-trafficking pathways.
source: ARF GTPases are often involved in membrane-trafficking pathways, while the subfamily of ARL proteins have more diverse functions (Burd et al., 2004; Sztul et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ARL proteins have more diverse functions than ARF GTPases.
source: ARF GTPases are often involved in membrane-trafficking pathways, while the subfamily of ARL proteins have more diverse functions (Burd et al., 2004; Sztul et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: CNNMs consist of an N-terminal extracellular domain, a transmembrane domain, and two cytosolic domains: a CBS-pair domain and a CNBH domain.
source: Structurally, CNNMs consist of an N-terminal extracellular domain, a transmembrane domain, and two cytosolic domains: a CBS-pair domain (also termed a Bateman domain) and a cyclic nucleotide-binding homology (CNBH) domain (de Baaij et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Two structures of prokaryotic CNNM orthologs have been determined, confirming that CNNMs are ion transporters.
source: Two structures of prokaryotic orthologs have been determined, confirming that the CNNMs are ion transporters (Chen et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: CNNM CBS-pair domains bind PRLs with low nanomolar affinity.
source: CNNM CBS-pair domains bind PRLs with low nanomolar affinity through an aspartic acid that inserts into the phosphatase catalytic site, mimicking a phosphoprotein substrate (Gehring et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: CNNM CBS-pair domains bind PRLs through an aspartic acid that inserts into the phosphatase catalytic site, mimicking a phosphoprotein substrate.
source: CNNM CBS-pair domains bind PRLs with low nanomolar affinity through an aspartic acid that inserts into the phosphatase catalytic site, mimicking a phosphoprotein substrate (Gehring et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: PRL binding to CNNMs regulates Mg2+ transport and promotes tumor progression in cancer.
source: The binding regulates Mg2+ transport and promotes tumor progression in cancer (Funato et al., 2014; Hardy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: ARL15 binds GTP with micromolar affinity.
source: Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) and NMR experiments demonstrate that ARL15 binds GTP with micromolar affinity, orders of magnitude weaker than typical GTPases.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated by ITC in Figure 1D showing a Kd of 20 µM.

claim: ARL15 binds GTP orders of magnitude weaker than typical GTPases.
source: Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) and NMR experiments demonstrate that ARL15 binds GTP with micromolar affinity, orders of magnitude weaker than typical GTPases.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by comparison to hRAS picomolar affinity mentioned in the text.

claim: ARL15 binds CNNM CBS-pair domains with low micromolar affinity.
source: We show that ARL15 binds CNNM CBS-pair domains with low micromolar affinity and inhibits CNNM2 Mg2+ efflux.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated by ITC experiments in Figure 2 showing Kd values of 1-2 µM.

claim: The ARL15-binding site on CNNMs overlaps with the PRL-binding site.
source: The structure shows that the ARL15-binding site overlaps with the previously identified PRL-binding site.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Loss of CNNM binding by ARL15 leads to a loss in the ability to suppress CNNM2 and TRPM7 channel activity.
source: Loss of CNNM binding leads to a loss in the ability of ARL15 to suppress CNNM2 and TRPM7 channel activity in cultured cells, confirming the biological relevance of the molecular interaction.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated by experiments with the R95A mutant in Figure 7.

claim: Full-length ARL15 showed a propensity to aggregate.
source: Full-length ARL15 showed a propensity to aggregate that hampered its analysis so a truncated version encompassing only the ARL15 GTPase domain (residues 32–197) was prepared.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing protein preparation.

claim: The N-terminal residues removed from ARL15 are the site of palmitoylation and promote membrane binding.
source: The N-terminal residues removed are the site of ARL15 palmitoylation and promote membrane binding (Wu et al., 2021), while C-terminal residues removed have no known function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: The C-terminal residues removed from ARL15 have no known function.
source: The N-terminal residues removed are the site of ARL15 palmitoylation and promote membrane binding (Wu et al., 2021), while C-terminal residues removed have no known function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The truncated ARL15 protein (residues 32-197) was stable and soluble at high micromolar concentrations.
source: The truncated protein was stable and soluble at high micromolar concentrations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing protein preparation.

claim: Initial attempts to preload ARL15 with GTP or GDP were unsuccessful.
source: Initial attempts to preload ARL15 with GTP or GDP were unsuccessful and suggested that ARL15 has weak binding affinity and was nucleotide-free when purified from Escherichia coli.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: ARL15 was nucleotide-free when purified from Escherichia coli.
source: Initial attempts to preload ARL15 with GTP or GDP were unsuccessful and suggested that ARL15 has weak binding affinity and was nucleotide-free when purified from Escherichia coli.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and confirmed by UV spectroscopy in Figure 1A.

claim: The UV spectrum of hRAS shows flat absorbance from 250 to 290 nm due to the presence of bound nucleotide.
source: The UV spectrum of hRAS is flat absorbance from 250 to 290 nm due to the presence of bound nucleotide while ARL15 shows a deep dip around 250 nm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ARL15 shows a deep dip around 250 nm in its UV spectrum.
source: The UV spectrum of hRAS is flat absorbance from 250 to 290 nm due to the presence of bound nucleotide while ARL15 shows a deep dip around 250 nm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The ARL15 sample showed no absorbance after heat denaturation and protein precipitation.
source: The ARL15 sample showed no absorbance after protein precipitation while the hRAS spectrum revealed the bound nucleotide.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The hRAS spectrum revealed bound nucleotide after heat denaturation.
source: The ARL15 sample showed no absorbance after protein precipitation while the hRAS spectrum revealed the bound nucleotide.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 2D NMR of 15N-labeled ARL15 (32–197) showed well-dispersed signals of equal intensity, characteristic of a well-folded, homogenous protein preparation.
source: 2D NMR of 15N-labeled ARL15 (32–197) showed well-dispersed signals of equal intensity, characteristic of a well-folded, homogenous protein preparation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Titration of ARL15 with GTP caused changes in the NMR spectrum in the slow-exchange NMR time scale.
source: Titration with GTP caused changes in the spectrum in the slow-exchange NMR time scale and a general improvement in strength and uniformity of the signals.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No 31P NMR signals were observed in ARL15 before GTP addition.
source: No 31P NMR signals were observed in the initial spectrum.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Upon addition of half an equivalent of GTP to ARL15, three broad signals from bound GTP phosphorus atoms appeared.
source: Upon addition of half an equivalent of GTP, three broad signals from bound GTP phosphorus atoms appeared.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Upon over titration of ARL15 with GTP, additional sharper peaks appeared that correspond to free (unbound) GTP.
source: Upon over titration, additional sharper peaks appeared that correspond to free (unbound) GTP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: After 14 hr incubation of ARL15 with GTP, a small signal from free phosphate was visible along with a 25% decrease in free GTP.
source: After 14 hr, a small signal from free phosphate was visible along with a 25% decrease in free GTP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The intrinsic GTPase activity of ARL15 corresponds to a turnover rate of 5×10–6 s–1.
source: Assuming the activity is not a contaminating bacterial enzyme, this corresponds to a turnover rate of 5×10–6 s–1 or roughly an order of magnitude smaller than the intrinsic GTPase activity of 7.1×10–5 s–1 of hRAS (Neal et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and calculated from data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The intrinsic GTPase activity of hRAS is 7.1×10–5 s–1.
source: Assuming the activity is not a contaminating bacterial enzyme, this corresponds to a turnover rate of 5×10–6 s–1 or roughly an order of magnitude smaller than the intrinsic GTPase activity of 7.1×10–5 s–1 of hRAS (Neal et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: ARL15 binds GTP with an affinity of 20 µM as measured by ITC.
source: A clear and unambiguous thermogram was observed with 300 µM ARL15 that could fit a single binding site model with an affinity of 20 µM (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The affinity of ARL15 for GTP is almost six orders of magnitude weaker than the picomolar affinity of hRAS.
source: This is almost six orders of magnitude weaker than the picomolar affinity of hRAS and other small GTPases (Ford et al., 2009; Neal et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: ITC experiments with CNNM2 CBS-pair domain (residues 429–584) and ARL15 (32–197) generated a strong exothermic signal corresponding to affinities of 1–2 μM.
source: ITC experiments with both constructs generated a strong exothermic signal when titrated with ARL15 (32–197), corresponding to affinities of 1–2 μM (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The presence of the CNBH domain did not significantly increase ARL15 binding affinity to CNNM2.
source: Unlike previous co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Zolotarov et al., 2021), we did not observe a significant increase in affinity when the CNBH domain was present (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ARL15 binds to CBS-pair domains of CNNM3 and CNNM4 with similar affinities to CNNM2.
source: Experiments with the CBS-pair domains of CNNM3 and CNNM4 showed similar binding affinities; addition of the CNBH domains had no effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ARL15 binds to the CBS-pair domain of CNNM1 with roughly 15-fold weaker affinity than to CNNM2.
source: ITC experiments with CBS-pair domain of CNNM1 also showed binding but with roughly 15-fold weaker affinity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ARL15 binding to CNNMs is a conserved property of CNNM proteins.
source: These results demonstrate that ARL15 binding is a conserved property of CNNM proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the binding data in Figure 2C.

claim: CNNM binding by ARL15 was not affected by the absence or presence of GTP.
source: Unexpectedly, CNNM binding was not affected by the absence or presence of GTP, while GDP addition had a minor effect, raising the Kd by about 40% (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GDP addition had a minor effect on ARL15-CNNM binding, raising the Kd by about 40%.
source: Unexpectedly, CNNM binding was not affected by the absence or presence of GTP, while GDP addition had a minor effect, raising the Kd by about 40% (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The ARL15 nucleotide-binding switch regions are not significantly involved in CNNM binding.
source: These results suggest that the ARL15 nucleotide-binding switch regions are not significantly involved in CNNM binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the nucleotide binding data.

claim: The addition of 5 mM EDTA to the binding buffer had no effect on ARL15-CNNM binding.
source: The addition of 5 mM EDTA to the binding buffer (which contained 1 mM Mg2+) had no effect on binding in agreement with co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Zolotarov et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A small, twofold improvement in ARL15-CNNM2 binding affinity was observed when ATP was present.
source: On the other hand, we observed a small, twofold improvement in affinity when ATP was present.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The CNNM2 T568I mutant bound ARL15 as well as the wild-type domain in the absence of ATP.
source: The mutant bound ARL15 as well as the wild-type (WT) domain in the absence of ATP, but it did not show increased affinity in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The CNNM2 T568I mutant did not show increased affinity for ARL15 in the presence of ATP.
source: The mutant bound ARL15 as well as the wild-type (WT) domain in the absence of ATP, but it did not show increased affinity in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A small amount of positive allosteric coupling exists between the CNNM2 ATP and ARL15-binding sites.
source: This confirmed that a small amount of positive allosteric coupling exists between the CNNM2 ATP and ARL15-binding sites.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the T568I mutant data.

claim: Crystals of ARL15-CNNM2 CBS-pair domain complex diffracted to 3.2 Å using synchrotron radiation.
source: The best crystals diffracted to 3.2 Å using synchrotron radiation (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 1.

claim: The structure of ARL15-CNNM2 CBS-pair domain complex was solved by molecular replacement.
source: The structure was solved by molecular replacement using the structure of the CNNM2 CBS-pair domain (PDB 4IY0) and an AlphaFold2 model of ARL15.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The large asymmetric unit of the ARL15-CNNM2 crystal contains four ARL15 and four CNNM2 CBS-pair domains.
source: The large asymmetric unit contains four ARL15 and four CNNM2 CBS-pair domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The relative position of the ARL15 molecules to CBS-pair domains was well defined with 0.6 Å RMSD between the four copies.
source: The relative position of the ARL15 molecules to CBS-pair domains was well defined with 0.6 Å RMSD between the four copies.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The protein interfaces in the ARL15-CNNM2 crystal structure were among the best-defined areas in the electron density map.
source: The protein interfaces were among the best-defined areas in the electron density map.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The CBS-pair domains are present as dimers with a small twist in the ARL15-CNNM2 crystal structure.
source: As is typical, the CBS-pair domains are present as dimers with a small twist, possibly due to the absence of Mg2+-ATP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The twist in the CBS-pair domain dimer generates two contact surfaces between the ARL15 and CNNM2 CBS-pair domains.
source: This twist generates two contact surfaces between the ARL15 and CNNM2 CBS-pair domains (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The larger ARL15-CNNM2 binding surface contains numerous polar contacts and involves a C-terminal part of helix α2 with following loop and the loop following helix α3 of ARL15.
source: The larger surface contains numerous polar contacts and involves two ARL15 structural elements: a C-terminal part of helix α2 with following loop and the loop following helix α3 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ARL15 helix α2 is a continuation of the Switch II region.
source: Helix α2 is a continuation of the Switch II region and is a common binding site for many GTPase effectors.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: ARL15 Gln98 makes intermolecular hydrogen bonds with CNNM2 Thr529 and the backbone amide of Phe526.
source: ARL15 Gln98 makes intermolecular hydrogen bonds with CNNM2 Thr529 and the backbone amide of Phe526.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ARL15 Gln131 and His129 form hydrogen bonds with CNNM2 backbone carbonyl of Phe524 and Leu522.
source: ARL15 Gln131 and His129 form hydrogen bonds with CNNM2 backbone carbonyl of Phe524 and Leu522.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In one copy of the ARL15-CBS complex, the side chain of Arg95 bonds with the backbone carbonyl of Tyr561.
source: In one copy of the ARL15-CBS complex, the side chain of Arg95 bonds with the backbone carbonyl of Tyr561.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: All the ARL15-CNNM2 interfaces show hydrophobic stacking between aliphatic part of Arg95 and the side chain of Phe524.
source: Significantly, all the ARL15-CNNM2 interfaces show hydrophobic stacking between aliphatic part of Arg95 and the side chain of Phe524.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: ARL15 Pro130 inserts into a small pocket formed by side chains of CNNM2 Pro521 and His523.
source: Another key hydrophobic binding determinant is provided by ARL15 Pro130 that inserts into a small pocket formed by side chains of CNNM2 Pro521 and His523.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The second binding surface between ARL15 and the CBS-pair domain involves ARL15 residues in the loop following helix α4.
source: The second binding surface between ARL15 and the CBS-pair domain is smaller and involves ARL15 residues in the loop following helix α4 that sit in a shallow pocket formed by two helices from the CBS-pair domain (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: An RMSD of ~1.5 Å was observed between ARL15 and the GTPases ARL2, ARL3, ARF1, and ARF6.
source: An RMSD of ~1.5 Å was observed between ARL15 and the GTPases ARL2, ARL3, ARF1, and ARF6, reflecting the high degree of sequence identity (around 35%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: ARL15 showed a large degree of disorder in the GTP-binding site and loop regions.
source: ARL15 showed a large degree of disorder in the GTP-binding site and loop regions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The GTP-binding site of ARL15 was unoccupied in the crystal structure despite the presence of a GTP analog in solution.
source: Although a GTP analog was present in the solution, the binding site was unoccupied, suggesting that nucleotide binding was incompatible with protein-protein contacts in the crystal.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The G1 motif (P-loop) of ARL15 was traceable but adopted a conformation incompatible with nucleotide binding.
source: The G1 motif (P-loop) was traceable but adopted a conformation incompatible with nucleotide binding while the G2 and G5 motifs were largely disordered.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The G2 and G5 motifs of ARL15 were largely disordered in the crystal structure.
source: The G1 motif (P-loop) was traceable but adopted a conformation incompatible with nucleotide binding while the G2 and G5 motifs were largely disordered.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: 1D NMR spectra of ARL15 mutants closely matched the spectrum of WT ARL15, confirming that the mutations did not cause protein unfolding.
source: 1D NMR spectra of the mutants closely matched the spectrum of WT ARL15 confirming that the mutations did not cause protein unfolding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pulldowns with GST-fused CNNM2 CBS-pair domain showed binding for WT ARL15 and the P163K mutant but not for S94K, R95A, and P130W.
source: Pulldowns with GST-fused CNNM2 CBS-pair domain showed binding for WT ARL15 and the P163K mutant but not for S94K, R95A, and P130W (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The R95A and P130W mutations abrogated ARL15 binding to CNNM2 CBS-pair domain.
source: The R95A and P130W mutations abrogated binding while S94K and S94W decreased the affinity of ARL15 by 20-fold (Kd of 40 μM).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: S94K and S94W mutations decreased the affinity of ARL15 for CNNM2 by 20-fold (Kd of 40 μM).
source: The R95A and P130W mutations abrogated binding while S94K and S94W decreased the affinity of ARL15 by 20-fold (Kd of 40 μM).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Mutation of Pro163 at the second interface had no effect on ARL15-CNNM2 binding.
source: On the other hand, mutation of Pro163 at the second interface had no effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: The P163K and P163W mutants showed WT affinity for the CNNM2 CBS-pair domain.
source: The P163K and P163W mutants showed WT affinity for the CNNM2 CBS-pair domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: The first interaction surface between ARL15 and CNNM is critical for binding while the second surface is dispensable.
source: These results establish that the first interaction surface is critical for the ARL15-CNNM binding while the second surface is dispensable and likely the result of crystal packing.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: The second interaction surface between ARL15 and CNNM is likely the result of crystal packing.
source: These results establish that the first interaction surface is critical for the ARL15-CNNM binding while the second surface is dispensable and likely the result of crystal packing.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the mutagenesis data.

claim: The GST-tagged CBS-pair domain of murine CNNM2 efficiently pulled down FLAG-tagged full-length ARL15.
source: The GST-tagged CBS-pair domain of murine CNNM2 efficiently pulled down FLAG-tagged full-length ARL15 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Native CNNM3 was efficiently co-immunoprecipitated by FLAG-tagged ARL15 WT but not FLAG-tagged ARL15 mutant (R95A).
source: Native CNNM3 was efficiently co-immunoprecipitated by FLAG-tagged ARL15 WT but not FLAG-tagged ARL15 mutant (R95A) or in untransfected cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Arg95 is essential for the interaction between ARL15 and full-length CNNM3.
source: Thus, Arg95 is essential for the interaction with full-length CNNM3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the co-IP data in Figure 4G.

claim: CNNM2 residues His523 and Phe524 make important contacts with ARL15 in the crystal structure.
source: CNNM2 residues His523 and Phe524 make important contacts with ARL15 in the crystal structure (Figure 3F and Figure 3—video 1) and are conserved from humans to flies (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CNNM2 residues His523 and Phe524 are conserved from humans to flies.
source: CNNM2 residues His523 and Phe524 make important contacts with ARL15 in the crystal structure (Figure 3F and Figure 3—video 1) and are conserved from humans to flies (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The CNNM1 C508F mutant showed a significantly stronger pulldown of ARL15 than did the WT domain.
source: The CNNM1 C508F mutant showed a significantly stronger pulldown of ARL15 than did the WT domain (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The CNNM1 C508F mutant binds ARL15 with an affinity of 9 µM, a threefold improvement over WT.
source: The increase in affinity was measured by ITC to be 9 µM, a threefold improvement over WT (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In CNNM1, the cysteine at position 508 is replaced by tryptophan in turtles and tortoises.
source: Interestingly, while the cysteine is perfectly conserved in mammals and most vertebrates, it is replaced by tryptophan in turtles and tortoises.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Weaker ARL15 binding appears to be a functional or conserved feature of CNNM1 proteins.
source: Weaker ARL15 binding appears to be a functional or, at least, a conserved feature of CNNM1 proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the conservation data.

claim: Mutation of either the phenylalanine or histidine residues in CNNM2, CNNM3, or CNNM4 caused a complete loss of ARL15 binding in pulldown assays.
source: Mutation of either the phenylalanine or histidine residues caused a complete loss of ARL15 binding to either the CBS-pair domains or larger cytosolic fragments including the CNBH domain in pulldown assays (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: The histidine mutants of CNNM2, CNNM3, and CNNM4 showed complete loss of ARL15 binding by ITC.
source: This was largely confirmed by ITC titrations, which showed complete loss of binding for the histidine mutants (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The phenylalanine mutants of CNNMs showed small enthalpic signals in the ITC thermograms, suggesting very weak binding.
source: The phenylalanine mutants showed small enthalpic signals in the ITC thermograms, suggesting very weak binding, but the affinities were too weak to be quantified.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: ARL15 binds identically to all four CNNM isoforms.
source: In summary, the mutagenesis results corroborate the binding surfaces observed in the crystal structure and the concurrence of the results across the four CNNM isoforms confirms that ARL15 binds identically to all the proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutagenesis data.

claim: Structural superposition of the complexes with the CNNM2 CBS-pair domain shows considerable overlap in positions of ARL15 and PRL1.
source: Structural superposition of the complexes with the CNNM2 CBS-pair domain shows considerable overlap in positions of ARL15 and PRL1 (Figure 6A and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ARL15 and PRL1 cannot bind CNNM2 at the same time.
source: Structural superposition of the complexes with the CNNM2 CBS-pair domain shows considerable overlap in positions of ARL15 and PRL1 (Figure 6A and Figure 6—video 1). This strongly suggests they cannot bind at the same time.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural overlap shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Titration of ARL15 into a mixture of CNNM2 CBS and PRL2 resulted in essentially no heat released, indicating no binding occurred.
source: Indeed, titration of ARL15 into a mixture of CNNM2 CBS and PRL2 resulted in essentially no heat released indicating no binding occurred (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PRL2 prevented the CBS-pair domain binding to ARL15 in NMR experiments.
source: In the spectrum with both PRL2 and the CBS-pair domain, all the NMR signals were visible (Figure 6C), thus showing that PRL2 prevented the CBS-pair domain binding to ARL15.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The CNNM2 D558A mutant bound to ARL15 with the same affinity as WT CBS-pair domain.
source: The D558A mutant bound to ARL15 with the same affinity as WT CBS-pair domain but was unable to interact with PRL2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The CNNM2 D558A mutant was unable to interact with PRL2.
source: The D558A mutant bound to ARL15 with the same affinity as WT CBS-pair domain but was unable to interact with PRL2.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The CNNM2 H523K mutant bound PRL2 with nanomolar affinity.
source: Conversely, the H523K mutant bound PRL2 with nanomolar affinity but completely blocked ARL15 binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The CNNM2 H523K mutant completely blocked ARL15 binding.
source: Conversely, the H523K mutant bound PRL2 with nanomolar affinity but completely blocked ARL15 binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Cells overexpressing CNNMs show Mg2+ efflux when in Mg2+-free solution.
source: Cells overexpressing CNNMs show Mg2+ efflux in cells when in Mg2+-free solution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: PRL3 inhibits CNNM4 activity by binding to the CBS-pair domain.
source: PRL3 inhibits CNNM4 activity by binding to the CBS-pair domain (Funato et al., 2014; Gulerez et al., 2016; Kozlov et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: CNNM2-expressing cells showed a 35% drop in Mg2+ levels.
source: CNNM2-expressing cells showed a 35% drop in Mg2+ levels, while untransfected cells showed little or no drop.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Untransfected cells showed little or no drop in Mg2+ levels in Mg2+-free solution.
source: CNNM2-expressing cells showed a 35% drop in Mg2+ levels, while untransfected cells showed little or no drop.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cells expressing both CNNM2 and ARL15 showed no Mg2+ efflux.
source: Cells expressing both CNNM2 and ARL15 showed no efflux, thus demonstrating that, like PRL3, ARL15 inhibits CNNM protein activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The inhibition of CNNM2 by ARL15 is due to ARL15 binding to the CBS-pair domain.
source: The ARL15 R95A mutant was unable to inhibit CNNM2 function confirming that the inhibition is due to ARL15 binding to the CBS-pair domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: CNNM2 localizes to the plasma membrane and an intracellular compartment, possibly the Golgi apparatus.
source: Confocal microscopy shows that CNNM2 localizes to the plasma membrane and an intracellular compartment, possibly the Golgi apparatus.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and shown in the confocal images.

claim: ARL15 expression does not affect CNNM2 localization.
source: This localization is not affected by ARL15 expression.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and shown in the confocal images.

claim: Both wild-type ARL15 and the R95A mutant localize to the plasma membrane as well as internal structures.
source: Both wild-type ARL15 and the R95A mutant localize to the plasma membrane as well as internal structures.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and shown in the confocal images.

claim: Overexpression of ARL15 inhibits Zn2+ influx in cells by TRPM7.
source: Overexpression of ARL15 has been shown to inhibit Zn2+ influx in cells by TRPM7 (Bai et al., 2021; Kollewe et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Co-expression of ARL15 suppresses TRPM7 ion influx in whole-cell electrophysiological recordings.
source: Whole-cell electrophysiological recordings of cells with and without co-expression of ARL15 confirmed that ARL15 suppresses ion influx (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: Co-expression of the ARL15 R95A mutant showed no suppression of TRPM7 currents.
source: In contrast, co-expression of the ARL15 R95A mutant showed no suppression with currents indistinguishable from the untransfected cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: ARL15 co-expression markedly decreased intracellular Zn2+ levels in TRPM7-expressing cells.
source: ARL15 co-expression markedly decreased intracellular Zn2+ levels in TRPM7-expressing cells while expression of the ARL15 R95A mutant had no effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: Expression of the ARL15 R95A mutant had no effect on intracellular Zn2+ levels in TRPM7-expressing cells.
source: ARL15 co-expression markedly decreased intracellular Zn2+ levels in TRPM7-expressing cells while expression of the ARL15 R95A mutant had no effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: ARL15 has an alanine at position 86 instead of the glutamine found in almost all other ARLs.
source: Notably, ARL15 has an alanine at position 86 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A). In almost all other ARLs, this position is occupied by glutamine, which plays a role in GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In almost all other ARLs, position 86 is occupied by glutamine, which plays a role in GTP hydrolysis.
source: Notably, ARL15 has an alanine at position 86 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A). In almost all other ARLs, this position is occupied by glutamine, which plays a role in GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by knowledge of GTPase mechanisms.

claim: It is questionable whether ARL15 has catalytic GTPase activity.
source: It is questionable whether ARL15 has catalytic activity, given the importance and prevalence of glutamine in related GTPases.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: Weak affinity of ARL15 for GTP is a property shared with several other ARL-family members.
source: Weak affinity of ARL15 for GTP is a property shared with several other ARL-family members.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: ARL2, ARL3, and ARL13B have been reported to bind guanine nucleotides with micromolar affinity.
source: ARL2, ARL3, and ARL13B have all been reported to bind guanine nucleotides with micromolar affinity (Gulerez et al., 2016; Linari et al., 1999; Ivanova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: It is unlikely a GEF is required to facilitate GTP binding to ARL15.
source: We see rapid binding of GTP to ARL15 in ITC experiments (Figure 1D), so it is unlikely a GEF is required to facilitate GTP binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the ITC data.

claim: In the presence of rapid exchange, ARL15 GTPase activity would constitute an unregulated, futile cycle depleting the cell of GTP.
source: It is impossible to affirm that a GAP does not exist for ARL15, but this seems unlikely since, in presence of rapid exchange, ARL15 GTPase activity would constitute an unregulated, futile cycle depleting the cell of GTP.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation about the biological implications.

claim: The connecting region between Switch I and Switch II in ARL15 contains two β-strands and a patch of three conserved aromatic residues.
source: This region is characteristic of ARF/ARL GTPase family members and contains two β-strands and a patch of three conserved aromatic residues that participate in the interactions with effectors (Ménétrey et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: In ARL15, the three conserved aromatic residues are Phe66, Lys81, and Tyr96.
source: In ARL15, the three residues are Phe66, Lys81, and Tyr96.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Lys81 in ARL15 replaces a tryptophan found in all ARFs and many ARLs.
source: Lys81 replaces a tryptophan found in all ARFs and many ARLs, which suggests that ARL15 interacts with effectors differently from other ARF/ARL GTPases.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: ARL15 interacts with effectors differently from other ARF/ARL GTPases.
source: Lys81 replaces a tryptophan found in all ARFs and many ARLs, which suggests that ARL15 interacts with effectors differently from other ARF/ARL GTPases.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the sequence differences.

claim: CBS-pair domains consist of repeated CBS motifs - CBS1 and CBS2 - that fold together to form a Mg2+-ATP binding site.
source: They consist of repeated CBS motifs - CBS1 and CBS2 - that fold together to form a Mg2+-ATP binding site (Ereño-Orbea et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: CNNM CBS-pair domains most often dimerize in a head-to-head manner forming a ring around two ATP molecules.
source: The CNNM CBS-pair domains most often dimerize in a head-to-head manner forming a ring around two ATP molecules but considerable plasticity exists at the dimerization interface with many different conformations observed in crystal structures (Corral-Rodríguez et al., 2014; Giménez-Mascarell et al., 2017; Gulerez et al., 2016; Hanzal-Bayer et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2020; Fakih et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Considerable plasticity exists at the dimerization interface of CNNM CBS-pair domains with many different conformations observed in crystal structures.
source: The CNNM CBS-pair domains most often dimerize in a head-to-head manner forming a ring around two ATP molecules but considerable plasticity exists at the dimerization interface with many different conformations observed in crystal structures (Corral-Rodríguez et al., 2014; Giménez-Mascarell et al., 2017; Gulerez et al., 2016; Hanzal-Bayer et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2020; Fakih et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: PRL-2 overexpression decreased ARL15 binding to CNNM3 and enhanced the function of TRPM7.
source: PRL-2 overexpression decreased ARL15 binding to CNNM3 and enhanced the function of TRPM7.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: In cells, competition between ARL15 and PRLs will be affected by relative abundance and post-translational modifications.
source: In cells, competition between the two proteins will be affected by relative abundance of ARL15 and PRLs and their post-translational modifications.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation about cellular regulation.

claim: Based on its ~100-fold higher affinity in vitro, PRLs should outcompete ARL15 for CNNM binding.
source: Based on its ~100-fold higher affinity in vitro, PRLs should outcompete ARL15 for CNNM binding but this would depend on the local protein concentrations.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the binding data.

claim: ARL15 is dynamically and reversibly membrane associated due to its palmitoylation.
source: ARL15 is dynamically and reversibly membrane associated due to its palmitoylation (Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: PRLs are membrane associated due to C-terminal farnesylation.
source: PRLs are similarly membrane associated due to C-terminal farnesylation (Cates et al., 1996; Zeng et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: PRLs undergo additional modifications of their catalytic cysteine which regulate their affinity for binding CNNM proteins.
source: PRLs undergo additional modifications of their catalytic cysteine which regulate their affinity for binding CNNM proteins (Gulerez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: ARL15 and a PRL could bind simultaneously to separate monomers of a CNNM dimer.
source: The dimeric nature of CNNM proteins adds an additional complication as ARL15 and a PRL could bind simultaneously to separate monomers of a CNNM dimer.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation about possible binding modes.

claim: PRLs inhibit Mg2+ efflux by CNNM4 through direct binding to the CBS-pair domain.
source: PRLs inhibit Mg2+ efflux by CNNM4 through direct binding to the CBS-pair domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: CNNMs are electroneutral ion antiporters.
source: CNNMs are electroneutral ion antiporters (Chen et al., 2021; Yamazaki et al., 2013) while TRPM7 is electrogenic (Monteilh-Zoller et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: TRPM7 is electrogenic.
source: CNNMs are electroneutral ion antiporters (Chen et al., 2021; Yamazaki et al., 2013) while TRPM7 is electrogenic (Monteilh-Zoller et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: Activating both CNNM and TRPM7 transporters simultaneously would constitute a futile Na+ leak and likely be deleterious.
source: Activating both transporters simultaneously would constitute a futile Na+ leak and likely be deleterious.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation about the biological implications.
